title: Starting a Child Care Agency in Tennessee: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

html:
Introduction

Starting a Child Care Agency in Tennessee represents a meaningful opportunity to serve children, including infants, toddlers, and those with special needs, while building a compliant, sustainable care business. The child care landscape in the Volunteer State is defined by high demand and a structured regulatory environment. Oversight and funding are administered by the Tennessee Department of Human Services (TDHS), which manages licensing and distributes state and federal funds to support quality care across the state.

With significant demand, with waitlists in major cities like Nashville exceeding 500 families and wait times of 6-12 months, and a state budget of approximately $319 million in CCDF funds for 2024, Tennessee offers a high-demand market with significant opportunities for providers who can meet quality standards and cater to specific niches. Providers who can successfully navigate the state’s Quality Rating and Improvement System (QRIS) can access reimbursement rates from $100 to $240 per week, creating a clear path to financial viability for those prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Child Care Agency in Tennessee, from understanding the regulations and licensing process with TDHS to developing a business plan, hiring staff, and preparing for your first inspection. Whether you are opening a small family child care home or a large commercial center, this comprehensive overview will provide the foundation you need for success.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Tennessee’s Child Care Agency Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Tennessee’s Child Care Agency Regulations

Navigating the regulatory landscape is the first and most critical step in opening your agency. Tennessee regulates Child Care Agencies through the Tennessee Department of Human Services (TDHS), which is responsible for setting standards for health, safety, and quality of care, conducting inspections, and issuing licenses to child care agencies. The primary goal of TDHS is to ensure that all children in licensed care are in safe, healthy, and educationally enriching environments.

Providers who intend to serve families receiving state subsidies must also comply with federal frameworks, primarily the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) regulations. These federal rules mandate specific health and safety training, comprehensive background checks, and unannounced inspections. Additionally, all providers must adhere to the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) to ensure accessibility for children and parents with disabilities, and HIPAA if handling protected health information.

The regulatory framework in Tennessee emphasizes child safety, staff-to-child ratios, curriculum quality, and facility compliance, all measured through the Quality Rating and Improvement System (QRIS). This system not only serves as a compliance benchmark but also directly impacts your reimbursement rates. Higher QRIS scores signal higher quality care and unlock higher payment tiers. Licenses are not permanent and typically require renewal every one to two years, contingent upon maintaining compliance and passing regular inspections.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Once you understand the regulatory environment, you must decide on the specific model of care you will provide. Tennessee supports multiple Child Care Agency variants, each with different licensing, staffing, and facility requirements. Choosing a niche can help you stand out in a competitive market and meet specific community needs.

Common program types and niches include:

  • Child Care Center: A facility-based program typically located in a commercial building, serving a larger number of children in age-specific groups.
  • Group Child Care Home: A program operated out of a residence, serving up to 12 children with a higher staff-to-child ratio than a family home.
  • Family Child Care Home: A program in the provider’s own residence, serving a smaller group of children (typically 5-7).
  • Special Needs Care: A specialized program designed to serve children with developmental, physical, or behavioral disabilities. This niche often qualifies for a 15% premium on state reimbursement rates.
  • Infant and Toddler Programs: Focusing exclusively on care for children from birth to 36 months. This requires specialized knowledge, lower staff-to-child ratios, and specific facility accommodations.
  • Extended Hours Care: Offering services during non-traditional hours, such as evenings, overnights, and weekends, to cater to parents with variable work schedules.

Program size typically ranges from small family-style homes serving under 10 children to large centers serving over 100 children. Demand is strongest in metropolitan areas like Nashville, Memphis, and Knoxville, where population growth and high employment rates fuel the need for quality child care. Conversely, rural or suburban counties may offer entry opportunities with less direct competition, though the private-pay market may be smaller.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Establishing a formal business entity is a prerequisite for licensure. Most providers in Tennessee operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC), S-Corporation, or Non-Profit organization. Each structure has different implications for liability, taxation, and governance, so consulting with a legal and financial advisor is highly recommended.

To become a licensed provider, you must complete several foundational steps:

  • Register your business with the Tennessee Secretary of State to create a legal entity.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS, which is necessary for hiring employees and filing taxes.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (errors and omissions), and workers’ compensation insurance.
  • Submit a comprehensive licensing application to the Tennessee Department of Human Services (TDHS). This application package includes your business plan, policy and procedure manual, staffing plan, facility details, and background checks for all principals.

Licensing timelines can vary based on the completeness of your application, the time required for background checks, and the scheduling of your initial facility inspection. In Tennessee, providers should anticipate that the process will generally range from 4 to 9 months from application submission to receiving your license to operate.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is your roadmap to a sustainable operation. It should detail your mission, service model, marketing strategy, and, most importantly, your financial projections. Startup costs for a Child Care Agency in Tennessee can vary dramatically based on whether you lease or purchase a property, the extent of renovations needed, and the scale of your program. Generally, startup costs typically range from $75,000 for a small, leased center to over $500,000 for a large, custom-built facility.

Operating expenses are a critical component of your financial plan. In child care, these are driven primarily by labor, with staffing representing 50-60% of total operating costs due to mandated staff-to-child ratios. Other major expenses include rent or mortgage, utilities, insurance, supplies, and food.

Your revenue will come from a mix of private-pay tuition and state subsidies. Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges in Tennessee include:

  • State Subsidy: $100 – $240 per week per child, based on the center’s QRIS score.
  • Special Needs Premium: An additional 15% on top of the base subsidy rate for qualifying children with documented needs.
  • Private Pay Tuition: Rates set by the provider, which often exceed state reimbursement levels, especially in high-demand urban areas like Nashville.

With a solid operational plan, providers operating at a target occupancy of 75-85% capacity can generally achieve 20-30% gross margins. A well-structured business plan will help you secure funding and guide your decisions as you work toward profitability, which most new agencies achieve within 12-18 months.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Your physical location must meet strict TDHS standards designed to ensure the health and safety of children. Whether you are using a commercial space or your own home, the facility must pass an on-site inspection before a license can be issued.

Key facility requirements in Tennessee include:

  • Minimum Square Footage: A required amount of usable indoor space per child (typically 35 square feet) to prevent overcrowding and allow for various activities.
  • Outdoor Play Area: A secure, fenced outdoor space with a minimum square footage per child (often 75 square feet) and age-appropriate, shock-absorbent surfacing under equipment.
  • Restroom Facilities: An adequate number of child-sized toilets and handwashing sinks that are easily accessible to children.
  • Health and Safety Features: Secure entry and exit points, covered electrical outlets, safe storage for hazardous materials, and compliance with local fire and health department codes.
  • Food Preparation Area: If meals are prepared on-site, the kitchen must meet health code standards for sanitation, food storage, and preparation.

When selecting a location, consider factors beyond the physical building. Proximity to residential neighborhoods, elementary schools, and major employers can drive enrollment. Ensure the property is properly zoned for child care use and that there is a sufficient local workforce to draw from.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your staff is the heart of your child care agency. TDHS sets specific qualifications and training requirements for all personnel to ensure they are prepared to provide a safe and nurturing environment. Maintaining proper staff-to-child ratios at all times is one of the most critical compliance areas.

Required roles in a Tennessee child care center typically include:

  • Center Director: The leader of the facility, who must meet specific educational qualifications (e.g., a degree in Early Childhood Education or a related field) and have administrative experience.
  • Lead Teachers: Responsible for a specific classroom or age group, these individuals must have credentials like a Child Development Associate (CDA) or a college degree in a relevant field.
  • Assistant Teachers / Aides: Support staff who work under the supervision of a lead teacher to help care for children and maintain ratios.
  • Support Staff: Depending on the size of your center, you may also need a cook, an administrative assistant, or janitorial staff.

All staff members must undergo comprehensive training. Key training requirements include initial orientation covering health, safety, and child abuse recognition and reporting; annual continuing education hours in child development; CPR and First Aid certification for designated staff; and comprehensive criminal background checks and fingerprinting prior to employment.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Written policies and procedures are the operational backbone of your agency. They ensure consistency, promote safety, and demonstrate compliance to TDHS surveyors. Tennessee requires licensed providers to develop and maintain a comprehensive manual that is accessible to both staff and parents.

At a minimum, your policy manual must cover:

  • Health and Safety Procedures: Detailed plans for illness exclusion, medication administration, emergency response (fire, tornado, lockdown), and sanitation.
  • Staffing and Supervision Plans: Policies outlining staff-to-child ratios for all age groups, supervision practices for indoor and outdoor play, and background check procedures.
  • Curriculum and Daily Activity Schedules: A description of your educational philosophy and a schedule of daily activities that includes a balance of active play, quiet time, meals, and learning.
  • Behavior Guidance and Discipline Policies: A positive, non-punitive approach to managing children’s behavior.
  • Parent Communication and Grievance Procedures: Protocols for daily communication, parent-teacher conferences, and resolving parental concerns.
  • Enrollment, Attendance, and Fee Collection Policies: Clear guidelines for admission, tracking attendance, and managing tuition and subsidy payments.

In addition to facility-wide policies, you must develop an individual care or service plan for each child. These plans should be created in partnership with parents and outline the child’s specific needs, goals, and any special instructions related to allergies, health, or development. These plans must be reviewed and updated regularly per state rules.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

With long waitlists in many parts of Tennessee, your primary marketing challenge may be managing demand rather than creating it. However, building a strong reputation and a consistent pipeline of referrals is essential for long-term stability, especially as you aim for full occupancy.

In the child care industry, referrals typically come from professional and community networks rather than large-scale advertising. Key referral sources include:

  • State Child Care Resource and Referral (CCR&R) Networks: TDHS funds these agencies to help parents find licensed care. Being listed and having a good relationship with your local CCR&R is crucial.
  • Local School Districts and Pediatricians: These professionals are often the first point of contact for families seeking care recommendations.
  • Corporate Partnership Programs: Partnering with large local employers to offer child care benefits can provide a steady stream of enrollees.
  • Online Directories and Parent Groups: Maintaining a professional presence on platforms like Winnie, Care.com, and local Facebook parent groups is vital for visibility.
  • Word-of-Mouth: Your best marketing tool is the recommendation of a satisfied parent. Focus on providing exceptional care, and your reputation will grow organically.

Successful providers in Tennessee focus on demonstrating compliance, responsiveness, and positive child outcomes rather than on consumer advertising. A high QRIS score, clean inspection reports, and glowing parent testimonials are your most powerful marketing assets.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Receiving your license is the beginning, not the end, of your compliance journey. Oversight is ongoing and includes both scheduled and unannounced inspections from Tennessee Department of Human Services (TDHS) licensing consultants. These surveyors will review your facility, records, and practices to ensure you are adhering to all state regulations.

Inspections are comprehensive and focus on areas where agencies most often fall short. Common deficiencies cited in Tennessee include:

  • Failure to maintain correct staff-to-child ratios, especially during transitions like drop-off, pick-up, and naptime.
  • Incomplete or expired staff files, such as missing background checks, training certificates, or health records.
  • Facility safety hazards, like uncovered electrical outlets, unsafe playground equipment, or improper storage of cleaning supplies.
  • Improper documentation, including inaccurate attendance records, incomplete incident reports, or missing fire drill logs.

To stay prepared, implement a system of continuous quality improvement. Conduct regular self-audits of your facility and files, provide ongoing training for staff, and maintain audit-ready documentation at all times. Viewing your licensing consultant as a partner in quality, rather than just an enforcer, can help you proactively address issues and maintain a strong compliance record.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

1. How long does it take to open a Child Care Agency in Tennessee?

From application submission to receiving your license, the process typically takes 4-9 months, depending on the completeness of your paperwork and inspection schedules. Most new agencies achieve financial break-even within 12-18 months of operation.

2. What licenses are required?

You need a Child Care Agency license from the Tennessee Department of Human Services (TDHS). The specific type of license (e.g., Family Child Care Home, Group Child Care Home, or Child Care Center) depends on the size, location, and nature of your program.

3. What reimbursement is available?

Reimbursement is available through the state’s child care subsidy program, funded by the CCDF. In Tennessee, rates range from $100 to $240 per week per child, tiered based on your facility’s QRIS score. A 15% reimbursement premium is also available for serving children with documented special needs.

Conclusion

Starting a Child Care Agency in Tennessee is a challenging yet immensely rewarding venture. The state’s growing population and strong demand create a fertile ground for new providers, but success is built on a foundation of regulatory understanding, careful planning, and operational discipline. By focusing on the quality standards set by TDHS, investing in qualified and well-trained staff, and building strong relationships with families and referral sources, you can position your agency for long-term success and make a lasting impact on your community.
